en: Itivuttaka 34 Dukanipāta, Paṭhamavagga Thus it was said by the Blessed One; having said this, the Well-Farer rose from his seat and entered his dwelling. Then, when the venerable Ānanda had understood that the Blessed One had risen from his seat and entered his dwelling, he approached the group of five monks. Having approached, he spoke thus to the group of five monks: "Friends, the Blessed One has risen from his seat and entered his dwelling. You may approach him, friends; when you have approached him, you will receive from the Blessed One a teaching on the Dhamma such as you have never heard before. "Yes, friend," replied the group of five monks to the venerable Ānanda. Then the venerable Ānanda approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, sat down to one side, and said to the Blessed One: "Venerable sir, the Blessed One has risen from his seat and entered his dwelling. May the Blessed One teach the Dhamma to the group of five monks; when they have heard the Dhamma from the Blessed One, they will attain the unsurpassed security from bondage, which is nibbāna. "Ānanda, suppose there were a man who had forgotten the way to a certain village or town, and another man were to say to him: 'Come, good man, this is the way to that village or town; go along this path. Then, as that man went along that path, he would see a footprint leading toward that village or town, and he would think: 'The man who showed me the way must surely have gone this way. And as he followed that path, he would see a second, then a third, then a fourth, then a fifth, then a sixth, then a seventh footprint leading toward that village or town, and he would think:

'The man who showed me the way must surely have gone this way. Then, having followed that path, he would see the village or town with its pinnacled gatehouses, its watchtowers, its ramparts, its parks, groves, ponds, and lotus-pools, and he would think: 'I am indeed near to that village or town; I shall certainly enter it. In the same way, Ānanda, the group of five monks is like a man who has forgotten the way. The Dhamma taught by me is like the footprint leading toward the village or town. Come, Ānanda, let us approach the group of five monks; when you have approached them, you will receive from the Blessed One a teaching on the Dhamma such as you have never heard before. "Yes, venerable sir," replied the venerable Ānanda to the Blessed One. Then the venerable Ānanda approached the group of five monks, paid homage to them, sat down to one side, and said to them: "Friends, the Blessed One has risen from his seat and entered his dwelling. May the Blessed One teach the Dhamma to you; when you have heard the Dhamma from the Blessed One, you will attain the unsurpassed security from bondage, which is nibbāna. "Friend Ānanda, do not trouble the Blessed One too soon; the Blessed One is weary. A second time... A third time, the venerable Ānanda said to the group of five monks: "Friends, the Blessed One has risen from his seat and entered his dwelling. May the Blessed One teach the Dhamma to you; when you have heard the Dhamma from the Blessed One, you will attain the unsurpassed security from bondage, which is nibbāna. And a third time, the group of five monks said to the venerable Ānanda: "Friend Ānanda, do not trouble the Blessed One too soon; the Blessed One is weary. Then the venerable Ānanda rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, and keeping him on his right, he departed. He approached the group of five monks, paid homage to them, sat down to one side, and said to them: "Friends, the Blessed One has risen from his seat and entered his dwelling. May the Blessed One teach the Dhamma to you; when you have heard the Dhamma from the Blessed One, you will attain the unsurpassed security from bondage, which is nibbāna. "Friend Ānanda, do not trouble the Blessed One too soon; the Blessed One is weary. For a second time... For a third time, the venerable Ānanda said to the group of five monks: "Friends, the Blessed One has risen from his seat and entered his dwelling. May the Blessed One teach the Dhamma to you; when you have heard the Dhamma from the Blessed One, you will attain the unsurpassed security from bondage, which is nibbāna. And for a third time, the group of five monks said to the venerable Ānanda: "Friend Ānanda, do not trouble the Blessed One too soon; the Blessed One is weary. Then the venerable Ānanda rose from his seat, paid homage to the group of five monks, and keeping them on his right, he departed. He approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, sat down to one side, and said to the Blessed One: "Venerable sir, the group of five monks says: 'Friend Ānanda, do not trouble the Blessed One too soon; the Blessed One is weary. "Ānanda, go to the group of five monks and say to them: 'Friends, the Teacher calls you; the Blessed One calls you. "Yes, venerable sir," replied the venerable Ānanda to the Blessed One. He approached the group of five monks, paid homage to them, stood to one side, and said to them: "Friends, the Teacher calls you; the Blessed One calls you. "Yes, friend," replied the group of five monks to the venerable Ānanda. They approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, and sat down to one side. Then the Blessed One addressed the group of five monks: "Monks, these two extremes should not be pursued by one who has gone forth into homelessness. Which two? The pursuit of sensual pleasure in sense-objects, which is low, vulgar, worldly, ignoble, and unbeneficial; and the pursuit of self-mortification, which is painful, ignoble, and unbeneficial. Monks, the Tathāgata has awakened to the middle way, which avoids these two extremes, and it gives vision, gives knowledge, and leads to peace, to direct knowledge, to enlightenment, and to nibbāna. And what, monks, is that middle way awakened to by the Tathāgata? It is the Noble Eightfold Path; that is, right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration. This, monks, is that middle way awakened to by the Tathāgata, which gives vision, gives knowledge, and leads to peace, to direct knowledge, to enlightenment, and to nibbāna. Now, monks, this is the noble truth of suffering: birth is suffering, aging is suffering, death is suffering; sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair are suffering; association with the unpleasant is suffering, separation from the pleasant is suffering, not getting what one desires is suffering—in short, the five aggregates of clinging are suffering. This, monks, is the noble truth of the origin of suffering: it is this craving that leads to renewed existence, accompanied by delight and lust, seeking delight here and there; that is, craving for sensual pleasures, craving for existence, and craving for cessation. This, monks, is the noble truth of the cessation of suffering: it is the remainderless fading away and cessation of that very craving, the giving up and relinquishing of it, freedom from it, and non-reliance on it. This, monks, is the noble truth of the way leading to the cessation of suffering: it is this Noble Eightfold Path; that is, right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration. "Now, monks, this noble truth of suffering is to be fully understood. This noble truth of the origin of suffering is to be abandoned. This noble truth of the cessation of suffering is to be realized. This noble truth of the way leading to the cessation of suffering is to be developed. "In regard to these four noble truths, monks, there is a first realization of knowledge; there is a second realization of knowledge; there is a third realization of knowledge; there is a fourth realization of knowledge. "And what, monks, is the first realization of knowledge? Here, monks, a noble disciple understands as it really is: 'This is suffering. He understands as it really is: 'This is the origin of suffering. He understands as it really is: 'This is the cessation of suffering. He understands as it really is: 'This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering. This, monks, is the first realization of knowledge. "And what, monks, is the second realization of knowledge? Here, monks, a noble disciple understands as it really is: 'This noble truth of suffering has been fully understood. This was said by the Blessed One, said by the Arahant; so I have heard:
"Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu who is not ardent and not fearful is incapable of enlightenment, incapable of Nibbāna, incapable of attaining the unsurpassed security from bondage."
“Monks, a monk who is ardent and who possesses a sense of moral dread is capable of awakening, capable of Nibbāna, capable of attaining the unsurpassed security from bondage.
Thus the Blessed One spoke. With reference to this, it is said:
“One who is without ardor and without fear of wrongdoing,
who is full of sloth and torpor— ”
a bhikkhu such as this is incapable of attaining supreme enlightenment.
But he who is mindful, wise, meditative,
having severed the fetter of birth and old age—
“Right here one may touch unsurpassed perfect enlightenment.
This meaning too was spoken by the Blessed One; thus have I heard.
